title: Pinchas: the five sisters (Numbers 27:1–11)
hookLine: Zelophehad's daughters ask to inherit; God tells Moses they speak right
tomorrow: Pinchas: a shepherd for the flock

lines: A RULE THAT LEAVES YOU OUT.
cards: A rule that has always been the rule, and it leaves someone out. It's easy to grumble about a rule like that at the kitchen table and leave it there.
The people are counted again, family by family, to divide the land ahead. The land will pass from fathers to sons.

And then five women walk up to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting and stand before Moses, Eleazar the priest, the chiefs and the entire community. Their names are Mahlah, Noa, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah.
Their father, Zelophehad, had no sons.

teach.h: DON'T LET OUR FATHER'S NAME DISAPPEAR.
teach.b: In paraphrase, they say: our father died in the wilderness. He wasn't part of Korach's rebellion; he died in his own sin. And he had no sons.
Why should our father's name disappear from his family just because he had no son? Give us a holding among our father's brothers. Notice how carefully they argue.
They ask first that their father's name not be erased. They head off the obvious objection: he wasn't a rebel. And they ask in public, before every authority at once.
He brings their case before God.

And God says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "The daughters of Zelophehad speak right." Give them their father's inheritance. Then something bigger: the answer becomes a law for everyone.
If a man dies without a son, his inheritance passes to his daughter. Five women at a tent changed the law for every family after them.

teach.h: ONE QUESTION, A LAW FOR ALL.
teach.b: The rabbis admired them enormously. The Talmud calls them wise, skilled at reading the law, and righteous, and says they chose their moment carefully, speaking when inheritance was already on the table.

Some sages added that this passage was meant to be written through them all along, as if God had been waiting for someone to ask. Their names appear several times in the Bible, and not always in the same order.
One teaching reads that as a sign that all five were equal.

how: The daughters of Zelophehad are read in the portion of Pinchas each summer, and their names, Mahlah, Noa, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, are named in full each time the story is read.

o: the father of five daughters who had no sons
the tent where the five sisters made their case
the portion where five sisters win the right to inherit

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: asked to inherit their father's land
wise, skilled in the law, righteous

s: the sisters argued that their father was not part of Korach's rebellion
they headed off the objection before anyone could raise it.
Moses decided their case himself on the spot
the answer applied only to Zelophehad's family
it became a law for everyone: with no son, the inheritance passes to a daughter.

games.q: you're one of five sisters. the law gives land only to sons, and your father had none. what do you do?
o: stand before Moses and the whole community and ask.
games.why: they asked, in public, at the Tent of Meeting. God said they speak right, and the law changed for every family.

practice: Think of one thing that feels unfair and that you've only complained about privately: a workload, a family arrangement, a policy.
Imagine standing at the tent like the five sisters, and find the first sentence, calm and clear, that names what's fair without attacking anyone.

carryVoice: Your line: the daughters speak right. One fair question, asked in the open, became a law for all. Day four hundred sixty-seven, done.
